intro: Saying what you like or hate doing is important when you introduce yourself, talk about hobbies or meet new people. After like, love, hate and enjoy, English usually uses the -ing form of the verb: “I love dancing”.
objectifs: Show your feelings from very positive to very negative (love, like, don't mind, hate, can't stand).
Use like / love / hate + -ing verb or + noun.
Ask and answer questions about free time (Do you like…? Yes, I do).

texte: Here are the most common verbs and expressions, from the most positive to the most negative. All of them can take a noun (I love music) or an -ing verb (I love dancing).
“I don't mind” means “it's OK for me, it's not a problem”: it is neutral. In conversation, “I can't stand” is stronger than “I hate”.

lignes: I really like reading. I enjoy walking.

sections.note: “I like Paul” means Paul is nice and you enjoy his company. “I love Paul” shows love (or very strong affection).

sections.titre: The structure: verb of feeling + -ing or + noun
texte: After like, love, hate, enjoy, don't mind, can't stand, use a noun or an -ing verb. Here the -ing verb works like a noun: “swimming” = the activity of swimming.
Use the present simple: remember the s with he / she / it (“She likes dancing”) and “do / does” for questions and negatives (“Does he like cooking?”, “He doesn't like cooking”).
With a noun in a general meaning, don't use an article: “I like dogs” (all dogs), “She loves music”.
exemples: Does your sister like travelling? — Yes, she does.
I don't mind working at the weekend.

texte: These are the same rules as for the present continuous (lesson 8). Usually you just add -ing.
If the verb ends in a silent e, drop the e. If a short verb ends in consonant + vowel + consonant, double the last consonant. If the verb ends in -ie, write -ying.

lignes: read → reading, play → playing, cook → cooking
dance → dancing, write → writing, ride → riding
swim → swimming, run → running, shop → shopping

texte: With like, love and hate, you can also use “to” + verb, especially in American English: “I like to swim”. For things you do for pleasure, British English prefers -ing: “I like swimming”. Both are correct.
But enjoy, don't mind and can't stand ALWAYS take -ing: “I enjoy cooking”, never “I enjoy to cook”.
Big trap: “would like” (= want, politely) takes “to”: “I'd like to go to the cinema” (lesson 34). Compare: “I like going to the cinema” (in general, I enjoy it).
exemples: I like swimming. / I like to swim.
I enjoy cooking for my friends.
I like dancing, but tonight I'd like to stay at home.

texte: The usual question is “What do you like doing in your free time?” or “What are your hobbies?”.
To react: “Me too!” after a positive sentence, “Me neither” after a negative sentence. Lesson 70 presents “So do I” and “Neither do I”.
“I like… very much” or “I really like…”: “very much” goes after the object, never between the verb and the object.
exemples: What do you like doing at the weekend? — I love going to the market.
Question and answer about free time.
I don't like shopping. — Me neither!
Me neither = I don't like it either.

formule: love / like / don't mind / hate / enjoy / can't stand + verb-ing (or + noun): I love dancing.
prononciation: The ending -ing is /ɪŋ/: a nasal sound at the back of the mouth, with no hard g at the end. “singing” = /ˈsɪŋɪŋ/.
“love” is /lʌv/: the vowel of “but”, not an o.
“I don't mind”: the t often disappears and the n becomes m: /aɪ dəʊm ˈmaɪnd/.
Stress the feeling and the activity: “I LOVE DANCING”, “I CAN'T STAND QUEUING”.
erreurs: I like swimming. / I like to swim.
Present simple: s with he / she / it.
Do you like reading? — Yes, I like.
Do you like reading? — Yes, I do.
I would like going to Canada.
I would like to go to Canada.

dialogue.contexte: In Ottawa, two students, Samira and Jake, are going to share a flat. They get to know each other.
lignes: So, what do you like doing in your free time?
I love cooking, especially Moroccan food. And I really enjoy hiking.
Great! I can't cook at all, but I love eating!
Ha! And you? What are your hobbies?
I like playing the guitar and watching hockey.
I don't mind music, but not at night, please!
Don't worry. Do you like cleaning? I hate cleaning.
Me too! Let's make a cleaning plan.
Me too = I hate it too.

mots: I enjoy walking by the sea.
an activity you do for pleasure
What do you do in your free time?
time when you are not working or studying
be unhappy about something (mostly in negatives and questions)
the activity of reading books and texts
She loves cooking for her family.
We go hiking in the mountains.
walking a long way in the country
I can't stand shopping on Saturdays.
the activity of buying things in shops

exercices.consigne: Put the verb in brackets in the right form.
Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I love reading. / I love to read.
She doesn't like at all shopping.
She doesn't like shopping at all.
Do you like swimming? / Do you like to swim?
I enjoy very much cooking for my friends.
I really enjoy cooking for my friends. / I enjoy cooking for my friends very much.

exercices.consigne: Write five sentences about what you like: use love, like, don't mind, don't like and hate (or can't stand), each with an -ing verb.
items: I love dancing at weddings. I like watching football with my friends. I don't mind cooking, but I don't like washing the dishes. I hate getting up early on Sundays, and I can't stand waiting for the bus in the rain.

a_retenir: love > like > don't mind > don't like > hate > can't stand, + -ing verb or + noun.
Present simple: She likes dancing. Does he like cooking? — Yes, he does.
Spelling: dance → dancing, swim → swimming, lie → lying, travel → travelling (US traveling).
enjoy, don't mind, can't stand: always + -ing; like / love / hate: -ing or to.
Careful: I like going (in general) ≠ I'd like to go (I want to, now).
